scribe_response.text: Tell me about a journey you have never forgotten. The journey um I have never forgotten happened when I was ten, on my father's boat. My father had built a fishing boat for a man on Guimaras Island, across the strait. He decided to deliver it himself, and to my surprise he asked me to come. My brothers were jealous, but I was the one who always um sat beside him in the um workshop. We left at dawn, with the sky streaked orange and the water flat as a mirror. My mother packed rice, grilled fish, and a thermos of sweet coffee wrapped in a towel. She gave me a straw hat and told me to behave like a um lady and not a seagull. The boat was painted bright blue, with a white stripe and a name on the bow. It was called um Maria Luisa, after the buyer's mother, and my father carved the letters himself. I sat on a small bench at the front as the little engine coughed to life. The wind smelled of salt and diesel, and the waves slapped the hull cheerfully. Behind us Iloilo grew smaller, until the church um towers looked like toys on a green tablecloth. My father stood at the tiller, humming his old tune about the fisherman and the moon. What happened next? For the first time I saw him as, as a man at home on the water. He pointed out um a school of flying fish leaping across the surface like silver arrows. I clapped so hard I nearly fell overboard, and he caught my dress, dress. He told me about the nights he um had fished with only a lantern and a net. He said the sea is like a good teacher, patient, um severe, and generous all at once. At midmorning a squall came up from the south, and the um sky turned the color of slate. The waves grew taller, and the little boat rocked until my stomach was near my ears. My father calmly tied a rope around my waist and fastened it to the bench. He told me to look at the horizon and uh sing, because singing children do not get sick. So I sang every hymn I knew, shouting into the wind, and he joined in. The rain came down in sheets, and we were soaked, laughing and shivering together. After an hour the storm passed, and a rainbow stretched across the water. I thought the whole world had been washed and was brand new. Can you tell me more about that? We reached Guimaras by early afternoon, and a crowd was waiting on the beach. The buyer, a short man in a straw hat, ran into the surf and kissed the bow. His wife gave us grilled squid, steamed cassava, and mangoes as sweet as honey. I uh ate until I could hardly move and fell uh asleep on a mat under a palm tree. When I woke, the sun was low, and my father sat watching the sea with a quiet smile. We returned on a crowded ferry, because the blue boat had stayed behind. I leaned against my father's shoulder while the lights of Iloilo twinkled across the dark water. He smelled of wood shavings and rain, and I felt entirely safe. That day taught me that courage can be learned by singing in a storm. It also taught me um that a parent and child can share a whole world in uh one day. My father has been gone for many years, but I still feel that rope around um my waist. Whenever I board a plane or a ferry, I hum his tune and watch the horizon. I think that journey was the beginning of every adventure I have had since. Maybe that is why I was never afraid to leave.
